body:
`VolumeInverseNorm` computes `‖V⁻¹r‖` with one reduction over a `KernelFunctionOperation`. Before, it scaled `r` by `V⁻¹` in place, took `norm(r)`, and scaled `r` back. That cost two extra read–write passes over the residual per CG iteration and perturbed `r` by rounding. `r` is now left bit-identical.

The distributed `norm` and `dot!` now accept any `DistributedAbstractField`, so they reduce operations across ranks. Closes #6170.

Immersed 320×320×2560 stretched grid per GPU, no preconditioner, 100 CG iterations per solve, H100s on one node:

| | `residual_norm` | CG iteration | time step |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 GPU, `main` | 6.80 ms | 35.0 ms | 11.99 s |
| 1 GPU, this PR | 2.75 ms | 31.0 ms | 10.63 s |
| 8 GPUs, `main` | 7.30 ms | 37.4 ms | 12.67 s |
| 8 GPUs, this PR | 3.44 ms | 33.4 ms | 11.43 s |

On 1 and 2 CPU ranks, CG iteration counts and solutions match `main`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

body:
During my profiling running Oceananigans on distributed GPU setups (specifically CUDA) I noticed that there were a number of instances where the host and device are synchronised (using `sync_device'). This is needed to ensure that the MPI communications (filling and sending of buffers) occurs _after_ the field has been updated. However these synchronisations prevent extra work from being sent to the GPU to mask communications, and also cause gaps in GPU utilisations when small kernels are run.

Since in this case most of the work is being done on the GPU, we have extra CPU resources that could be used. On top of this, CUDA.jl has an API for creating events in the stream which can be used to check when kernels have finished running. This PR will attempt to use these events with asynchronous threads to handle the buffer filling and mpi comms in the background, allowing the main thread to keep adding work to the GPU until it needs the MPI comms to be completed.

Currently the benchmark pipeline script keeps only the rank 0 results. This causes issues when comparing to #5888 where the partitions are not equal in size, causing the throughput to look worse when it is actually improved.

By combining the results we can instead compare the total throughput across all the ranks, which is what we care about for scaling anyway.
